\chapter{All of Us}
\label{ch:bn-all-of-us}
\hlchaptermodality{35}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about more than one of us, more than one of you and more than one of them, and say what belongs to any of those groups.}

The plural ending taught two chapters earlier on nouns turns out to build every plural pronoun in the language without one exception, and a different ending replaces it when the pronoun has to own something — the first sight of the rule that the back slot holds one suffix at a time.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[āmrā]{\bn{আমরা} (āmrā) — we}

\label{lesson:BN-C24-amra}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{I}. Then make \textbf{\bn{ভাই}} plural, and say which group of nouns is allowed that ending.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the word that asks \emph{what is this?} — \emph{eṭā ki}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{আমরা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আমরা} \bn{ভালো}} — \emph{āmrā bhālo} — \textbf{we are well.}
\end{quote}

Look at what has happened. \textbf{\bn{আমি}} plus the living plural \textbf{-\bn{রা}} is \textbf{\bn{আমরা}}, and there is nothing else to learn: a pronoun is a living noun, so it takes the living noun's ending.

English cannot show you this. \emph{I} becomes \emph{we}, two words with no letter in common, and a learner has to memorise the pair. Bengali charges you nothing, because you paid two chapters ago.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: exclusive or inclusive? Bengali does not say}]
Some languages have two words for \emph{we} — one that includes the person you are talking to and one that shuts them out. Bengali has one, exactly as English does, and leaves it to context:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আমরা} \bn{ভালো}} can mean \emph{we (you and I) are well} or \emph{we (my family, not you) are well.}
\end{quote}

Nothing marks the difference. When it matters, a Bengali speaker names the group: \textbf{\bn{আমরা}}, and then who.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āmrā bhālo}
  \item the singular and the plural — \emph{āmi bhālo}, \emph{āmrā bhālo}
  \item the same ending on a noun — \emph{bhāirā}
  \item naming the group — \emph{āmrā}, \emph{āmār pôribār}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pieces is \textbf{\bn{আমরা}} made of? (\textbf{\bn{আমি}} and the living plural \textbf{-\bn{রা}}.) Why that ending and not the other one? (\textbf{A person is \bn{জীব}}.) And does Bengali have two words for \emph{we}? (\textbf{No} — one, like English.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tomrā]{\bn{তোমরা} (tomrā) — you, more than one}

\label{lesson:BN-C24-tomra}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{we}. Then say the plain word for \textbf{you} and the careful one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{তোমরা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{তোমরা} \bn{ভালো}} — \emph{tomrā bhālo} — \textbf{you are all well.}
\end{quote}

Same ending again. \textbf{\bn{তুমি}} plus \textbf{-\bn{রা}}, with the vowel settling to \textbf{\bn{তোম}-}, and Bengali has a word English lacks: \emph{you}, plural, unambiguously.

The careful rung pluralises too:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{তুমি}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{তোমরা}} — you, plainly
  \item \textbf{\bn{আপনি}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{আপনারা}} — you, respectfully
\end{itemize}

Four words where English has one, and every one of them is that same \textbf{-\bn{রা}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the grid, complete for two of three persons}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{one} & \textbf{more than one} \\
\midrule
I & \textbf{\bn{আমি}} & \textbf{\bn{আমরা}} \\
you, plainly & \textbf{\bn{তুমি}} & \textbf{\bn{তোমরা}} \\
you, carefully & \textbf{\bn{আপনি}} & \textbf{\bn{আপনারা}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One ending, applied without exception. Nothing here is irregular, which is worth saying out loud because the equivalent English table is nothing but exceptions.

The third row is the next lesson.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tomrā bhālo}
  \item singular then plural — \emph{tumi bhālo}, \emph{tomrā bhālo}
  \item the careful pair — \emph{āpni}, \emph{āpnārā}
  \item to a room of friends — \emph{tomrā}, \emph{āmār bôndhurā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the plural of \textbf{\bn{আপনি}}? (\textbf{\bn{আপনারা}}.) How many words does Bengali need where English says \emph{you}? (\textbf{Four} — two rungs, two numbers.) And which ending builds every one of them? (\textbf{-\bn{রা}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tārā]{\bn{তারা} (tārā) — they}

\label{lesson:BN-C24-tara}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{you, all of you}. Then say \textbf{he is well}, plainly.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{তারা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{তারা} \bn{ভালো}} — \emph{tārā bhālo} — \textbf{they are well.}
\end{quote}

The stem of \textbf{\bn{সে}} is \textbf{\bn{তা}-} — you saw it last chapter inside \textbf{\bn{তার}} — and with the living plural on the end it is \textbf{\bn{তারা}}. The careful form does what you would now expect: \textbf{\bn{তাঁরা}}, with the moon-dot.

That completes the grid. Six persons, in a language that spent thirty-three chapters able to talk about two:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{one} & \textbf{more than one} \\
\midrule
I & \textbf{\bn{আমি}} & \textbf{\bn{আমরা}} \\
you, plainly & \textbf{\bn{তুমি}} & \textbf{\bn{তোমরা}} \\
you, carefully & \textbf{\bn{আপনি}} & \textbf{\bn{আপনারা}} \\
he, she, plainly & \textbf{\bn{সে}} & \textbf{\bn{তারা}} \\
he, she, carefully & \textbf{\bn{তিনি}} & \textbf{\bn{তাঁরা}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one ending did all of it}]
Read the right-hand column downwards and every entry ends the same way. There is no irregular plural anywhere in the Bengali pronoun system — no \emph{I/we}, no \emph{he/they}, nothing to memorise as a pair.

And it is the same \textbf{-\bn{রা}} that pluralises \textbf{\bn{ভাই}} and \textbf{\bn{বোন}}. One rule, learned once, for people and for pronouns alike, because Bengali does not think those are different kinds of word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tārā bhālo}
  \item the careful one — \emph{tā̃rā bhālo}
  \item the three plurals in a row — \emph{āmrā}, \emph{tomrā}, \emph{tārā}
  \item the same ending on a noun — \emph{bônerā}
  \item singular against plural, all three persons — \emph{āmi/āmrā}, \emph{tumi/tomrā}, \emph{she/tārā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What stem is \textbf{\bn{তারা}} built on? (\textbf{\bn{তা}-}, the stem of \textbf{\bn{সে}}.) Is there an irregular plural pronoun in Bengali? (\textbf{No} — every one takes \textbf{-\bn{রা}}.) And what is the careful form? (\textbf{\bn{তাঁরা}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āmāder]{\bn{আমাদের} (āmāder) — our}

\label{lesson:BN-C24-amader}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{my}, \textbf{your} and \textbf{his}. Then say \textbf{we}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{আমাদের}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{আমাদের} \bn{পরিবার}} — \emph{āmāder pôribār} — \textbf{our family.}
\end{quote}

Here is the piece that finishes the possessive column. Watch what happens to the plural ending:

\textbf{\bn{আমরা}} $\to$ \textbf{\bn{আমাদের}}, not \emph{āmrār}.

The \textbf{-\bn{রা}} does not survive. In its place comes \textbf{-\bn{দের}}, which is the plural possessive ending and is used across the board:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{mine} & \textbf{ours} \\
\midrule
I / we & \textbf{\bn{আমার}} & \textbf{\bn{আমাদের}} \\
you, plainly & \textbf{\bn{তোমার}} & \textbf{\bn{তোমাদের}} \\
he, she / they & \textbf{\bn{তার}} & \textbf{\bn{তাদের}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one suffix at a time}]
This is the first sight of a rule that governs the whole back end of a Bengali word: \textbf{the slot holds one ending, and only one.} Plural and possessive cannot both be there, so a single ending is used that carries both meanings at once.

You have already seen the same economy without being told: \textbf{\bn{গুলো}} does plural \emph{and} definite, so it occupies the place \textbf{\bn{টা}} would otherwise have taken. Bengali merges endings where English would stack them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āmāder pôribār}
  \item the whole column — \emph{āmār}, \emph{tomār}, \emph{tār}, \emph{āmāder}, \emph{tomāder}, \emph{tāder}
  \item the ending that vanishes — \emph{āmrā}, but \emph{āmāder}
  \item their brothers — \emph{tāder bhāirā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to \textbf{-\bn{রা}} when a possessive is needed? (\textbf{It is replaced} by \textbf{-\bn{দের}}.) How many endings may the back slot hold at once? (\textbf{One.}) And which ending you already knew does two jobs for the same reason? (\textbf{\bn{গুলো}} — plural and definite.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āmrā · tomrā · tārā · āmāder]{All of us}

\label{lesson:BN-R24-all-of-us}



\begin{quote}
One ending made every plural pronoun in this chapter, and a different one made every plural possessive. Name both, and say why they cannot appear together.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the six persons — \emph{āmi}, \emph{āmrā}, \emph{tumi}, \emph{tomrā}, \emph{she}, \emph{tārā}
  \item the careful rungs — \emph{āpni}, \emph{āpnārā}, \emph{tini}, \emph{tā̃rā}
  \item the whole possessive column — \emph{āmār}, \emph{tomār}, \emph{tār}, \emph{āmāder}, \emph{tomāder}, \emph{tāder}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — four chapters back, and everything since}
Four chapters ago the letter \textbf{\bn{ট}} did not exist in this book and nothing could be pointed at, counted, pluralised or owned by anybody but you and the person in front of you. Run the whole distance, cold.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{ট}, then \bn{টা}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the classifier and the indefinite — \emph{jāmāṭā}, \emph{ekṭā jāmā}, \emph{ārekṭā jāmā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} pointing near and far — \emph{ei jāmāṭā}, \emph{oi jāmāṭā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the two plurals, sorted by group — \emph{bhāirā}, \emph{jāmāgulo}, \emph{chokhgulo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} an adjective that never changes — \emph{lāl jāmā}, \emph{lāl jāmāgulo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the third person, both rungs — \emph{she bhālo}, \emph{tini bhālo}, \emph{o bhālo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} whose, singular and plural — \emph{tār pôribār}, \emph{āmāder pôribār}, \emph{tāder bhāirā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the whole queue, with an owner on the front — \emph{āmāder ei lāl jāmāṭā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} asking about it — \emph{eṭā ki?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending makes every plural pronoun? (\textbf{-\bn{রা}}.) What replaces it when the pronoun has to own something? (\textbf{-\bn{দের}}.) Is any Bengali plural pronoun irregular? (\textbf{No.}) And which ending you met four chapters ago does two jobs for exactly the same reason? (\textbf{\bn{গুলো}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
